title: Why Your Students Should Decide When To Leave Time-Out eave-time-out/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that most teachers keep students in time-out for too short a period and make the mistake of deciding themselves when a student is ready to return. He recommends a minimum fifteen-minute time-out after which students, rather than the teacher, signal readiness to rejoin the class by raising a hand and requesting to return. He details four benefits of this student-centered approach: it offers students trust and ownership, it raises the level of accountability, it functions as an implicit act of contrition, and it removes the guesswork teachers otherwise face in judging whether a consequence 'worked.' He concludes that this method deepens the contrast between the discomfort of time-out and the privilege of full class membership, creating genuine behavioral leverage.
points: Time-out should last at least fifteen minutes, longer than the five-to-ten-minute norm most teachers use.
After the initial period, students — not the teacher — should signal when they are ready to return to class, by raising a hand and requesting permission.
Letting students decide when to leave time-out sends a message of trust and increases their sense of accountability for their own behavior.
The approach removes teacher guesswork about whether a consequence actually achieved its purpose.
Widening the gap between the discomfort of time-out and the privilege of full class membership creates genuine behavioral leverage.
quotes: Most teachers don’t keep their students in time-out long enough. Five to ten minutes seems to be the norm, but to be most effective, your students need to sit and reflect on their misbehavior for at least fifteen minutes.
It’s best to allow your students to decide when they’re ready to leave time-out.

When you give your students the responsibility to let you know when they’re ready to leave time-out, it causes them take ownership of their misbehavior and stirs in them the desire to care and to want to follow your rules.
Giving students the power to decide when to return to class burdens them with a greater level of accountability—making them active rather than passive participants in their improvement.
When you use a specific time period, or your best hunch, to determine when to remove students from time-out, you don’t have any idea if the consequence was effective. It’s a guessing game.
